bmt-2012-tournament-r1-02.title: Combine the logarithms
bmt-2012-tournament-r1-02.body:
Since $1=\log_x x$, the second bracket is $\log_x x+\log_x y+\log_x z=\log_x(xyz)$. Also $\log_{xyz}(x^z)=z\log_{xyz}x$. Therefore the product is
$$z\cdot\log_{xyz}x\cdot\log_x(xyz)=z\cdot 1=z=340,$$
because $\log_{xyz}x\cdot\log_x(xyz)=1$.

**Answer: 340**

bmt-2012-tournament-r1-03.title: Inclusion-exclusion
bmt-2012-tournament-r1-03.body:
Sequences with no A: $3^6=729$. Sequences with no U: $3^6=729$. Sequences with neither A nor U: $2^6=64$.

By inclusion-exclusion the number with no A's or no U's is $729+729-64=1394$.

**Answer: 1394**

bmt-2012-tournament-r1-05.title: Similar triangles
bmt-2012-tournament-r1-05.body:
Let the altitude from the right angle meet the hypotenuse $c$ at a point dividing it into $y$ (next to leg $b$) and $c-y$. The right triangle with hypotenuse $b$ and the full triangle share the angle $\theta$ between $b$ and $c$, so $\cos\theta=\frac bc=\frac yb$, giving $yc=b^2$.

The rectangle $R$ has width $y$ and height $c$, so its area is $yc=b^2=32^2=1024$.

**Answer: 1024**

bmt-2012-tournament-r1-06.title: Fix coordinates
bmt-2012-tournament-r1-06.body:
The vertices of a $5$-cube are the strings $(x_1,\dots,x_5)\in\{0,1\}^5$. A $k$-cube in it is obtained by fixing all but $k$ of the coordinates and letting the other $k$ vary freely. There are $\binom5k$ ways to choose the free coordinates and $2^{5-k}$ ways to fix the rest, so there are $\binom5k2^{5-k}$ $k$-cubes.

For $k=3$: $\binom53\cdot2^2=10\cdot4=40$.

**Answer: 40**

bmt-2012-tournament-r2-01.title: Linearity of expectation
bmt-2012-tournament-r2-01.body:
A given bin is empty iff all $4$ balls avoid it, which has probability $\left(\frac56\right)^4$. By linearity of expectation the expected number of empty bins is $6\cdot\left(\frac56\right)^4=\frac{625}{216}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{625}{216}$**

bmt-2012-tournament-r2-03.title: Angle chase
bmt-2012-tournament-r2-03.body:
Let $\angle BAE=\angle EAC=\alpha$ and $\angle BCA=\beta$, so $2\alpha+\beta=90^\circ$. Since $BD\perp AC$, $\angle ABD=\beta$ and $\angle DBC=90^\circ-\beta=2\alpha$, hence $\angle DBF=\angle FBC=\alpha$.

Then $\angle ABF=\angle ABD+\angle DBF=\beta+\alpha$. Also $\angle AFB$ is an exterior angle of triangle $BFC$, so $\angle AFB=\angle FBC+\angle FCB=\alpha+\beta$.

Thus triangle $ABF$ is isosceles with $AB=AF$. The line $AG$ bisects its apex angle $\angle BAF$, so it is also the median: $G$ is the midpoint of $BF$. Therefore $\dfrac{BG}{GF}=1$ (a coordinate computation with the given side lengths agrees).

**Answer: 1**

bmt-2012-tournament-r2-04.title: Polynomial division
bmt-2012-tournament-r2-04.body:
$n^2-2012=(n+7)(n-7)-1963$, so $\dfrac{n^2-2012}{n+7}=n-7-\dfrac{1963}{n+7}$. This is an integer iff $n+7\mid1963$. The largest divisor of $1963$ is $1963$ itself, giving $n=1963-7=1956$.

**Answer: 1956**

bmt-2012-tournament-r2-05.title: Put one vertex at a vertex of the pentagon
bmt-2012-tournament-r2-05.body:
The largest triangle has one vertex at a vertex $V_0$ of the pentagon and is symmetric about the axis of the pentagon through $V_0$ (a numerical search over all positions and orientations confirms this).

Let the pentagon be $V_0V_1V_2V_3V_4$ and let $Q$ be the triangle's vertex on side $V_1V_2$. The side $V_0V_1$ makes an angle of $54^\circ$ with the axis (half of the interior angle $108^\circ$), and the triangle's side $V_0Q$ makes an angle of $30^\circ$ with it, so $\angle V_1V_0Q=24^\circ$.

In triangle $V_0V_1Q$: $V_0V_1=1$ and $\angle V_0V_1Q=108^\circ$, so $\angle V_0QV_1=180^\circ-24^\circ-108^\circ=48^\circ$. By the law of sines,
$$V_0Q=\frac{\sin108^\circ}{\sin48^\circ}=\frac{\sin72^\circ}{\sin48^\circ}\approx1.2798.$$

**Answer: $\dfrac{\sin72^\circ}{\sin48^\circ}\approx1.2798$**

bmt-2012-tournament-r2-06.title: Coupon collector
bmt-2012-tournament-r2-06.body:
When she already has $k$ distinct notes, each new ball gives a new note with probability $\frac{7-k}{7}$, so the expected number of balls needed to get the next new note is $\frac{7}{7-k}$. Summing over $k=0,\dots,6$:
$$7\left(1+\frac12+\frac13+\frac14+\frac15+\frac16+\frac17\right)=7\cdot\frac{363}{140}=\frac{363}{20}=18.15.$$

**Answer: $\dfrac{363}{20}$**

bmt-2012-tournament-r3-01.title: Pair each subset with its reflection
bmt-2012-tournament-r3-01.body:
The map $x\mapsto2013-x$ sends a subset $K$ to a subset $K'$ with $A(K')=2013-A(K)$. So the set $R$ of averages is closed under $a\mapsto2013-a$, and pairing each value $a$ with $2013-a$ (they have average $\frac{2013}{2}$) shows $A(R)=\dfrac{2013}{2}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{2013}{2}$**

bmt-2012-tournament-r3-02.title: Relative motion
bmt-2012-tournament-r3-02.body:
The minute hand gains on the hour hand by $360^\circ\cdot\left(1-\frac1{12}\right)$ per hour, i.e. $11$ full relative revolutions every $12$ hours. In each relative revolution the angle between the hands is $90^\circ$ twice (once at $+90^\circ$ and once at $+270^\circ$). So in $12$ hours there are $22$ right angles, and in a full day $44$.

**Answer: 44**

bmt-2012-tournament-r3-03.title: Count the face-up cards
bmt-2012-tournament-r3-03.body:
Penny takes any $18$ cards as one pile (the other pile has $34$) and **turns that pile over**. Suppose the $18$ cards contained $x$ face-up cards (and $18-x$ face-down). Then the $34$ other cards contain $18-x$ face-up cards. After turning the first pile over it has $18-x$ face-up cards (the former face-down ones), and so both piles have exactly $18-x$ face-up cards.

**Answer: one pile of $18$ cards and one of $34$ cards**

bmt-2012-tournament-r3-04.title: Use the roots
bmt-2012-tournament-r3-04.body:
Let the roots be $n-1,n,n+1$. By Vieta, $a=-3n$ and $b=(n-1)n+n(n+1)+(n-1)(n+1)=3n^2-1$. Then
$$\frac{a^2}{b+1}=\frac{9n^2}{3n^2}=3$$
for every admissible $n\ne0$, so the maximum is $3$.

**Answer: 3**

bmt-2012-tournament-r3-05.title: Symmetry
bmt-2012-tournament-r3-05.body:
Let $B_n$ and $G_n$ be the numbers of blue and gold balls after $n$ iterations. The rules are symmetric under swapping colours, and the bag starts with one of each, so $E[B_n]=E[G_n]$. Each iteration adds exactly one ball, so $B_n+G_n=n+2$. Hence $2E[B_n]=n+2$ and
$$E[B_{525600}]=\frac{525602}{2}=262801.$$

**Answer: 262801**

bmt-2012-tournament-r4-01.title: Count the multiplicity of each term
bmt-2012-tournament-r4-01.body:
In $S_1+\cdots+S_{n-1}$ the term $\frac1j$ appears in $S_j,\dots,S_{n-1}$, that is $n-j$ times. In $nS_n$ it appears $n$ times. So the difference has $\frac1j$ with coefficient $n-(n-j)=j$, giving
$$\sum_{j=1}^n j\cdot\frac1j=n=144169.$$

**Answer: 144169**

bmt-2012-tournament-r4-02.title: Coordinates
bmt-2012-tournament-r4-02.body:
Put the large circle (diameter $AC$) at the origin with radius $6$, so $A=(-6,0)$, $B=(-2,0)$, $C=(6,0)$. The other circles are centred at $(-4,0)$ with radius $2$ and at $(2,0)$ with radius $4$.

A circle of radius $r$ centred at $(x,y)$ tangent internally to the big circle and externally to the two small ones satisfies
$$x^2+y^2=(6-r)^2,\quad (x+4)^2+y^2=(2+r)^2,\quad (x-2)^2+y^2=(4+r)^2.$$
Subtracting the first from the second: $8x+16=16r-32$, so $x=2r-6$. Subtracting the first from the third: $-4x+4=20r-20$, so $x=6-5r$. Hence $2r-6=6-5r$ and $r=\dfrac{12}7$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{12}{7}$**

bmt-2012-tournament-r4-03.title: Binomial theorem and telescoping
bmt-2012-tournament-r4-03.body:
Over all $i$ with $0\le i\le2^{n}-1$ ($n=576$ binary digits), $\sum x^{s(i)}=(1+x)^n$, since there are $\binom nk$ numbers with $k$ ones. Removing $i=2^n-1$ (which has $s=n$) leaves $(1+x)^n-x^n$.

The sum over $x=1,\dots,314$ telescopes:
$$\sum_{x=1}^{314}\left((x+1)^n-x^n\right)=315^{576}-1.$$
Now $629=17\cdot37$ and $\varphi(629)=16\cdot36=576$. Since $\gcd(315,629)=1$ ($315=3^2\cdot5\cdot7$), Euler's theorem gives $315^{576}\equiv1\pmod{629}$, so the result is $0$.

**Answer: 0**

bmt-2012-tournament-r4-04.title: Affine map to a square
bmt-2012-tournament-r4-04.body:
Area ratios are preserved by affine maps, so take $ABCD$ to be the unit square $A=(0,0)$, $B=(1,0)$, $C=(1,1)$, $D=(0,1)$, and let $\varepsilon=\frac1{42}$. Then $E=(\varepsilon,0)$, $F=(1-\varepsilon,1)$, $G=(1,\varepsilon)$, $H=(0,1-\varepsilon)$.

Intersecting the lines $CE$, $BH$, $DG$, $AF$ gives (with denominator $3445=41^2+42^2$)
$$M=\tfrac{(1723,\,1681)}{3445},\ N=\tfrac{(1764,\,1723)}{3445},\ P=\tfrac{(1722,\,1764)}{3445},\ Q=\tfrac{(1681,\,1722)}{3445}.$$
Consecutive differences are $\frac{(41,42)}{3445},\frac{(-42,41)}{3445},\dots$: perpendicular and equal in length, so $MNPQ$ is a square with side$^2=\frac{41^2+42^2}{3445^2}=\frac1{3445}$.

In general the ratio is $\dfrac1{k^2+(k-1)^2}$, so $\dfrac{S_1}{S}=\dfrac1{3445}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac1{3445}$**

bmt-2012-tournament-r4-05.title: Depends only on the set of primes
bmt-2012-tournament-r4-05.body:
$\dfrac n{\varphi(n)}=\prod_{p\mid n}\dfrac p{p-1}$, which depends only on the set of prime factors and increases when a prime is added. Five distinct primes need $n\ge2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11=2310>500$, so $n$ has at most $4$ distinct primes, and the best four are $2,3,5,7$ (ratio $\frac{2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7}{1\cdot2\cdot4\cdot6}=\frac{35}8$); any other set of four primes gives a smaller ratio.

The $n\le500$ with prime set $\{2,3,5,7\}$ are $210$ and $420$. Their sum is $630$.

**Answer: 630**

bmt-2012-tournament-r4-06.title: Split the path into straight runs
bmt-2012-tournament-r4-06.body:
The path has $11$ moves right and $11$ moves down. Exactly $6$ turns means $7$ straight runs alternating in direction.

If he starts moving right, the runs are R, D, R, D, R, D, R: $4$ right runs (positive lengths summing to $11$: $\binom{10}{3}=120$ ways) and $3$ down runs ($\binom{10}{2}=45$ ways), giving $120\cdot45=5400$ paths. Starting with a down move is symmetric: another $5400$.

Total: $2\cdot5400=10800$.

**Answer: 10800**

bmt-2012-tournament-r5-01.title: Find $n$, then use CRT
bmt-2012-tournament-r5-01.body:
For odd $n$ the alternating sum is $\frac{n+1}2$, so $\frac{n+1}2=2012$ and $n=4023=27\cdot149$.

We need $4^{2012}=2^{4024}$ modulo $27$ and modulo $149$.

- Mod $27$: $2$ has order $18$ and $4024\equiv10\pmod{18}$, so $2^{4024}\equiv2^{10}=1024\equiv25$.
- Mod $149$: the order divides $148$ and $4024\equiv28\pmod{148}$, so $2^{4024}\equiv2^{28}$. $2^8=256\equiv107$, $2^{16}\equiv107^2=11449\equiv125$, $2^{24}\equiv125\cdot107\equiv114$, $2^{28}\equiv114\cdot16=1824\equiv36$.

Solve $x\equiv25\pmod{27}$, $x\equiv36\pmod{149}$: $x=781$ ($781=28\cdot27+25=5\cdot149+36$).

**Answer: 781**

bmt-2012-tournament-r5-02.title: Add the three angles
bmt-2012-tournament-r5-02.body:
Put $A=(0,0)$, $B=(1,0)$, $C=(2,0)$, $D=(3,0)$ and $P=(0,1)$. Then $\angle PBA=45^\circ$, $\tan\angle PCA=\frac12$ and $\tan\angle PDA=\frac13$. Since
$$\tan(\angle PCA+\angle PDA)=\frac{\frac12+\frac13}{1-\frac16}=1,$$
$\angle PCA+\angle PDA=45^\circ$. The total is $45^\circ+45^\circ=90^\circ$.

**Answer: $90^\circ$**

bmt-2012-tournament-r5-03.title: Compose $f$ with itself
bmt-2012-tournament-r5-03.body:
The expression is $\dfrac{9(x-1)^2}{(x-4)^2}$. Since $f(x)=\dfrac3{x-1}$,
$$f(f(x))=\frac{3}{\frac3{x-1}-1}=\frac{3(x-1)}{3-(x-1)}=\frac{3(x-1)}{4-x}.$$
Squaring: $\big(f(f(x))\big)^2=\dfrac{9(x-1)^2}{(4-x)^2}=\dfrac{9(x^2-2x+1)}{x^2-8x+16}$, the given expression.

(Equivalently, with $f=f(x)$ we have $x-1=\frac3f$, so the expression is $\dfrac{9\cdot9/f^2}{(3/f-3)^2}=\dfrac{9}{(1-f)^2}$.)

**Answer: $\big(f(f(x))\big)^2$**

bmt-2012-tournament-r5-04.title: Coordinates
bmt-2012-tournament-r5-04.body:
The hypotenuse is $AC=17$, $BD=\frac{15\cdot8}{17}=\frac{120}{17}$, $AD=\frac{225}{17}$, $DC=\frac{64}{17}$. Put $D$ at the origin with $A=(-\frac{225}{17},0)$, $C=(\frac{64}{17},0)$, $B=(0,\frac{120}{17})$.

The inradius of the right triangle $ADB$ is $\frac{AD+BD-AB}{2}=\frac{45}{17}$, so $E=(-\frac{45}{17},\frac{45}{17})$; for $BDC$ it is $\frac{BD+DC-BC}2=\frac{24}{17}$, so $F=(\frac{24}{17},\frac{24}{17})$.

Intersecting line $EF$ with $BC$ and $AB$ gives $G=(\frac{960}{289},\frac{240}{289})$ and $H=(-\frac{1800}{289},\frac{1080}{289})$. One checks $BG^2=BH^2=BD^2=\frac{14400}{289}$, and $BG\perp BH$ (the angle at $B$ is $90^\circ$), so $BGH$ is an isosceles right triangle with legs $BD$:
$$[BGH]=\frac{BD^2}{2}=\frac{7200}{289}.$$

**Answer: $\dfrac{7200}{289}$**

bmt-2012-tournament-r5-05.title: Linearity of expectation
bmt-2012-tournament-r5-05.body:
There are $\binom{10}{6}$ choices of $6$ positions. For any such choice, the $6$ values in those positions are in decreasing order with probability $\frac1{6!}$. So the expected number is $\dfrac{\binom{10}6}{6!}=\dfrac{210}{720}=\dfrac7{24}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac7{24}$**

bmt-2012-tournament-r5-06.title: Track the increase when each cube is placed
bmt-2012-tournament-r5-06.body:
When the $i$-th cube is placed on a square that already has $x$ cubes, the score increases by $(x+1)^2-x^2=2x+1$. The previous $i-1$ cubes are in squares $1,\dots,i-1$, and the cube goes to a uniformly random one of the $i$ squares $1,\dots,i$, so the expected $x$ is $\frac{i-1}{i}$ (the average pile size over $i$ squares holding $i-1$ cubes). The expected gain is $2\cdot\frac{i-1}{i}+1$.

Summing over $i=1,\dots,6$: $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^6\left(3-\frac2i\right)=18-2H_6=18-2\cdot\frac{49}{20}=\frac{131}{10}$.

(Enumerating all $6!=720$ equally likely placements confirms $13.1$.)

**Answer: $\dfrac{131}{10}$**

bmt-2012-tournament-ch-02.title: Work up from the smallest die
bmt-2012-tournament-ch-02.body:
Let $E_n$ be the optimal expected score starting with an $n$-sided die. With a $2$-sided die she must keep the roll: $E_2=\frac32$. With $n$ sides she keeps a roll $v$ exactly when $v>E_{n-1}$ and otherwise rerolls.

- $E_3$: keep $2,3$, reroll $1$ (since $E_2=1.5$): $E_3=\frac{2+3}{3}+\frac13\cdot\frac32=\frac{13}6$.
- $E_4$: keep $3,4$ (since $E_3\approx2.17$): $E_4=\frac{3+4}4+\frac24\cdot\frac{13}6=\frac{17}6$.
- $E_5$: keep $3,4,5$ ($E_4\approx2.83$): $E_5=\frac{3+4+5}5+\frac25\cdot\frac{17}6=\frac{53}{15}$.
- $E_6$: keep $4,5,6$ ($E_5\approx3.53$): $E_6=\frac{4+5+6}6+\frac36\cdot\frac{53}{15}=\frac{64}{15}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{64}{15}$**

bmt-2012-tournament-ch-03.title: Factor $f(x)-7$
bmt-2012-tournament-ch-03.body:
$f(x)-7$ is a monic degree-$6$ polynomial with roots $1,2,3,4,5,6$, so $f(x)-7=(x-1)(x-2)\cdots(x-6)$. The coefficient of $x^5$ is minus the sum of the roots: $a=-(1+2+3+4+5+6)=-21$.

**Answer: $-21$**

bmt-2012-tournament-ch-04.title: Reduce and solve
bmt-2012-tournament-ch-04.body:
Dividing by $4$, the condition says $5a+3b$ and $5b-3a$ are powers of $2$. If $a,b$ were both even, then $\frac a2,\frac b2$ would also work (and $a+b$ not a power of $2$ is preserved under halving), with smaller sum; so for a minimal solution $a,b$ are not both even. Since $5a+3b$ is even, $a$ and $b$ are both odd.

Write $5a+3b=2^m$ and $5b-3a=2^n$. Adding, $2a+8b=2^m+2^n$. As $a,b$ are odd, $2a+8b\equiv2\pmod4$, so $2^m+2^n$ has exactly one factor $2$, which forces $\min(m,n)=1$. Since $5a+3b\ge8$, $n=1$: $5b-3a=2$.

Then $b\equiv1\pmod3$, and with $b$ odd, $b=6c+1$, $a=10c+1$. Now $5a+3b=68c+8=2^m$, so $17c+2=2^{m-2}$, i.e. $2^{m-2}\equiv2\pmod{17}$. The order of $2$ mod $17$ is $8$, so $m-2\equiv1\pmod8$. The value $m-2=1$ gives $c=0$, $a=b=1$ with $a+b=2$ a power of $2$ (excluded); the next is $m-2=9$: $17c+2=512$, $c=30$. Thus $a=301$, $b=181$ and $a+b=482$, which is not a power of $2$.

A computer search over all $a,b<700$ confirms that $482$ is the minimum.

**Answer: 482**

bmt-2012-tournament-ch-05.title: Inscribed angle
bmt-2012-tournament-ch-05.body:
Since $CDEF$ is a rhombus, $DE=DC$, and $DA=DC$ since $ABCD$ is a square. So $A$, $C$, $E$ all lie on the circle centred at $D$ with radius $DC$. The central angle $\angle ADC=90^\circ$, and $E$ lies on the major arc $AC$ (as $\angle CDE=144^\circ$ puts it outside the quadrant $ADC$), so the inscribed angle is $\angle AEC=\frac12\cdot90^\circ=45^\circ$.

**Answer: $45^\circ$**

bmt-2012-tournament-ch-06.title: Classify the configurations
bmt-2012-tournament-ch-06.body:
Label the coins $1,2,3,4$ around the square. Up to rotation and swapping heads/tails, an unsolved configuration is one of three kinds: **D** (two opposite coins differ from the other two, a diagonal pattern), **A** (two adjacent coins differ from the other two), or **S** (one coin differs from the other three). Moves available to Harry (up to symmetry): flip a diagonal pair, flip an adjacent pair, flip a single coin (flipping the complementary set is equivalent).

Harry cannot see, and Tom can rotate the card after every failed attempt, so Harry must use a fixed sequence that wins from every possible start. The sequence

diagonal pair ($2,4$), adjacent pair ($3,4$), diagonal pair, single coin, diagonal pair, adjacent pair, diagonal pair

works: the first move wins if the card was of kind D; kind A is eventually won by an adjacent-pair move when the pair happens to be aligned (a misaligned adjacent pair turns A into D, which the next diagonal move wins); kind S is untouched by diagonal and adjacent moves (they keep it of kind S), so the single-coin flip wins it or turns it into kind D or A, which the final moves finish. In total at most $7$ moves.

A breadth-first search over all sets of possible configurations (against every possible rotation by Tom) shows that no strategy with fewer than $7$ moves guarantees a win, so Harry always wins, in at most $7$ moves.

**Answer: 7**

bmt-2012-tournament-co-01.title: Two increasing blocks
bmt-2012-tournament-co-01.body:
Exactly one descent means the sequence is an increasing block followed by an increasing block, with a descent in between. Choose which elements go in the first block: any subset $A$ of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ (the rest form the second block); that is $2^n$ choices. Each choice gives one sequence (each block written increasingly), and different subsets $A$ give different sequences with at most one descent, except that the $n+1$ subsets $A=\{1,\dots,j\}$, $j=0,\dots,n$, all give the identity sequence $1,2,\dots,n$, which has no descent. Every other subset gives a sequence with exactly one descent, and distinct subsets give distinct sequences.

So the count is $2^n-(n+1)=2^n-n-1$. (Check: $n=2,3,4,5$ gives $1,4,11,26$.)

**Answer: $2^n-n-1$**

bmt-2012-tournament-co-02.title: Count by the longest side
bmt-2012-tournament-co-02.body:
Let the sides be $a\le b\le c$ with $a+b+c=2012$. The triangle inequality $a+b>c$ gives $c<1006$, i.e. $c\le1005$, and $c\ge\lceil2012/3\rceil=671$. For a fixed $c$, we need $a\le b=2012-a-c$, i.e. $a\le\frac{2012-c}2$, and $b\le c$, i.e. $a\ge2012-2c$.

So $a$ ranges over $2012-2c\le a\le\left\lfloor\frac{2012-c}2\right\rfloor$, which has $\frac{3c}2-1005$ values for even $c$ and $\frac{3c-1}2-1005$ for odd $c$.

- Even $c=672,\dots,1004$ ($167$ values): the counts are $3,6,\dots,501$, summing to $\frac{(3+501)\cdot167}2=42084$.
- Odd $c=671,\dots,1005$ ($168$ values): the counts are $1,4,\dots,502$, summing to $\frac{(1+502)\cdot168}2=42252$.

Total: $42084+42252=84336$. (A direct computer count agrees.)

**Answer: 84336**

bmt-2012-tournament-co-03.title: Determine the possible $x$
bmt-2012-tournament-co-03.body:
$\dfrac x{\varphi(x)}=\prod_{p\mid x}\dfrac p{p-1}$. For this to equal $3$ we need $\prod p=3\prod(p-1)$. Each odd prime contributes an even factor $p-1$ on the right, while the left side has a factor $2$ at most once, so $2$ must divide $x$ and there is at most one odd prime. Then $2p=3(p-1)$ gives $p=3$. So $S=\{2^i3^j: i,j\ge1\}$ (and indeed $\frac{2\cdot3}{1\cdot2}=3$).

$$\sum_{x\in S}\frac1x=\left(\sum_{i\ge1}\frac1{2^i}\right)\left(\sum_{j\ge1}\frac1{3^j}\right)=1\cdot\frac12=\frac12.$$

**Answer: $\dfrac12$**

bmt-2012-tournament-co-04.title: Induction on blocks of $2^n$
bmt-2012-tournament-co-04.body:
Let $T_n=f(1)+\cdots+f(2^n)$. The odd numbers up to $2^n$ contribute $1+3+\cdots+(2^n-1)=4^{n-1}$, and the even numbers $2m$ ($m\le2^{n-1}$) contribute $f(m)$, so $T_n=4^{n-1}+T_{n-1}$ with $T_0=1$. Hence $T_n=1+\dfrac{4^n-1}3$, and $T_5=1+341=342$.

Now $f(1)+\cdots+f(30)=T_5-f(31)-f(32)=342-31-1=310$.

**Answer: 310**

bmt-2012-tournament-co-05.title: Similar triangles and a geometric series
bmt-2012-tournament-co-05.body:
For a triangle with base $b$ and altitude $h$, the inscribed square with a side on the base has side $x$ satisfying $\frac xb=\frac{h-x}h$, so $x=\frac{bh}{b+h}$. The part of the triangle above this square is similar to the original, with base $b'=b\cdot\frac h{b+h}$ and height $h'=h\cdot\frac h{b+h}$. So the $k$-th square has side $b\,r^k$ with $r=\frac h{b+h}=\frac{100}{318}$.

The sum of the areas is $\displaystyle\sum_{k\ge1}b^2r^{2k}=\frac{b^2r^2}{1-r^2}=\frac{b^2h^2}{(b+h)^2-h^2}=\frac{bh^2}{b+2h}=\frac{218\cdot10000}{418}=\frac{1090000}{209}.$

**Answer: $\dfrac{1090000}{209}$**

bmt-2012-tournament-co-06.title: Tangents at the ends of a focal chord
bmt-2012-tournament-co-06.body:
Let the directrix be $D$, and drop perpendiculars $P_1D_1$, $P_2D_2$ to it. By the definition of the parabola, $P_iF=P_iD_i$, and the tangent at $P_i$ bisects $\angle D_iP_iF$. Let $\angle D_1P_1F=2\alpha$ and $\angle D_2P_2F=2\beta$. Because $P_1D_1\parallel P_2D_2$ (both perpendicular to the directrix) and $P_1,F,P_2$ are collinear, co-interior angles give $2\alpha+2\beta=180^\circ$, so $\alpha+\beta=90^\circ$.

The two tangents make angles $\alpha$ and $\beta$ with the chord $P_1P_2$, so in triangle $P_1QP_2$ the angle at $Q$ is $180^\circ-\alpha-\beta=90^\circ$.

(One can check that $P_1=(2,-22)$ is indeed on the parabola: $24-56+10=-22$.)

**Answer: $90^\circ$**
